question: A 55-year-old asthmatic patient goes to the ER with an exacerbation. One hour after the administration of supplemental oxygen and two nebulizations of salbutamol the patient does not improve. On examination, he breathed at 42 rpm with supraclavicular drainage and presented disseminated inspiratory and expiratory wheezing. The peak flow has dropped from 310 to 220 L / min. A gasometry extracted with oxygen at 28% shows a pO2 of 54 mmHg and a pCO2 of 35 mmHg. Which of the following attitudes seems LESS indicated?

options.opc: Nebulize ipratropium bromide together with salbutamol every 20 minutes.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Patient has severe asthma exacerbation" -> "Supplemental oxygen and salbutamol administered" -> "No improvement after one hour" -> "Respiratory rate at 42 rpm" -> "Supraclavicular retractions present" -> "Wheezing noted on examination" -> "Peak flow decreased from 310 to 220 L/min" -> "pO2 at 54 mmHg indicates severe hypoxemia" -> "pCO2 at 35 mmHg suggests no hypercapnia" -> "Increasing oxygen flow may worsen CO2 retention" -> "Less indicated to increase oxygen flow" -> 85%

analysis: The patient is experiencing a severe asthma exacerbation with significant respiratory distress, evidenced by high respiratory rate, low peak flow, and hypoxemia. While increasing oxygen flow is generally indicated in cases of hypoxemia, the other options involve more aggressive treatments for severe asthma. Administering intravenous magnesium can help in severe cases, and nebulizing ipratropium bromide can provide additional bronchodilation. Methylprednisolone is also appropriate for reducing inflammation. However, starting non-invasive mechanical ventilation (NIV) is less indicated at this stage, as it is typically reserved for cases of respiratory failure or when the patient is unable to maintain adequate ventilation, which is not clearly indicated here. Therefore, the least indicated option is starting non-invasive mechanical ventilation.
